concept.technique_name: sentence logic via clue-word direction matching

examples.problem_statement: The (i) ______ of Vladimir Nabokov as one of North America's literary giants has thrown the spotlight on his peripheral activities and has thus served to (ii) ______ his efforts as an amateur entomologist. Blank (i): A stigmatization, B lionization, C marginalization. Blank (ii): D foreground, E transcend, F obscure.

solution.operation: Reduce the sentence to its claim: something that happened to Nabokov has called attention to some of his peripheral activities.
solution.result: Both blanks must carry a 'calling attention to' direction.
solution.description: Strip the sentence to its core assertion first, so that each blank can be judged against a single directional requirement rather than against the vocabulary in isolation.

solution.operation: Test blank (i): reject 'stigmatization' and 'marginalization' because each represents a turning away from him, not a calling attention to him.
solution.result: Choice B, lionization, survives, since to lionize means to treat as important.
solution.description: Eliminate the two blank (i) options whose direction is away from attention; the remaining word is the one that matches the attention-calling direction the sentence requires.

solution.operation: Use the given fact that Nabokov is a literary giant to classify entomology as one of his peripheral activities, then fill blank (ii) with a word meaning 'call attention to'.
solution.description: Identify which activity the spotlight falls on, then pick the blank (ii) word whose meaning matches the spotlight relationship the sentence has already set up.

solution.operation: Check the rejected blank (ii) options: spotlighting something would not result in transcending it or obscuring it.
solution.result: E and F are ruled out, confirming B and D.
solution.description: Confirm the choice by testing the two discarded words against the spotlight image, so the answer rests on elimination as well as on selection.

examples.answer: Choice B: lionization; Choice D: foreground

key_reminders: Either blank may be the starting point; begin with whichever one the sentence's own logic pins down.
The connective 'and has thus served to' forces both blanks to point in the same direction.
A word is correct only if it matches the sentence's direction, not merely its topic.
common_mistakes: Reading 'peripheral activities' as a negative cue and choosing marginalization for blank (i).
Choosing 'obscure' for blank (ii) because entomology is peripheral, ignoring that the spotlight clause reverses that direction.

concept.technique_name: ordering powers by substituting small natural numbers

examples.problem_statement: If A = n^{(2n)^n}, B = n^{n^{2n}}, C = (n^{2n})^n and D = (n^n)^{n^2}, where n is a natural number and n \neq 1, arrange A, B, C and D in terms of their values.

solution.description: Substitute the smallest permitted value of n into A and B and reduce each tower to a single power of 2; the two agree, so equality is possible between them.
Do the same substitution for C and D at n = 2; these two also collapse to the same power, so equality is possible between them as well.

solution.result: B > A > D > C at n = 3
solution.description: Move to the next value of n to break the ties; with a common base of 3 the four expressions are ranked simply by comparing their exponents.

solution.operation: Verify that the same ranking holds for n = 4 and merge it with the n = 2 equalities.
solution.description: Confirm the n = 3 pattern persists at n = 4, then combine it with the equalities found at n = 2 so the equal signs appear only where the n = 2 case demands them.

key_reminders: Powers of the same base are ordered by comparing their exponents alone.
A tower must be collapsed from the top down before the exponents can be compared.
Equalities at one value of n and strict inequalities at larger n combine into a \geq relation.
common_mistakes: Testing only n = 2, where A = B and C = D, and concluding all four are pairwise equal.
Reading A as n^{2n \cdot n} instead of collapsing (2n)^n first, which changes the ranking.

concept.technique_name: part : part : whole ratio with an unknown multiplier

examples.problem_statement: Laura established a new flower garden, planting 4 tulip plants to every 1 rose plant, and no other plants. If she planted a total of 50 plants in the garden, how many of those plants were tulips?

solution.description: Extend the given part-to-part ratio into a part : part : whole ratio by adding the two parts, since the question asks about a total rather than about roses.

solution.operation: Write the ratio with an unknown integer multiplier x:\ 4x : 1x : 5x
solution.description: Attach a common multiplier to every term so the ratio becomes actual plant counts that still sit in the required proportion.
Set the whole term equal to the 50 plants actually planted and solve for the multiplier, which is the single unknown linking the ratio to the real counts.
Substitute the multiplier back into the tulip term, since the question asks for tulips and not for the multiplier itself.

key_reminders: A part : part ratio becomes a part : part : whole ratio by summing the parts.
Every term of a ratio shares one unknown integer multiplier.
Solve for the multiplier first, then substitute it into the term the question asks about.
common_mistakes: Dividing 50 by 4 instead of by 5, using the tulip part in place of the whole.
Stopping at x = 10 and reporting the multiplier rather than 4x.
